content: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is defined as the presence of urticaria (hives), angioedema, or both, persisting for six weeks or longer. This condition is more commonly observed in adults than in children, and women are affected more frequently than men. The diagnosis of CSU is primarily clinical, based on the episodic appearance of characteristic urticarial lesions, with or without angioedema, on most days of the week for a duration of six weeks or more. In 80–90% of adults and children with CSU, no specific underlying cause can be identified. Routine skin biopsy is not required for the diagnosis of CSU. However, it may be indicated in cases where urticarial vasculitis is suspected, or in rare patients with features suggestive of mastocytosis. Investigative tests for understanding the pathogenesis of CSU include the autologous serum skin test (ASST), autologous plasma skin test (APST), assays for autoantibodies against immunoglobulin E (IgE) or Fc-epsilon-RI, and in vitro assessments of basophil function. However, these tests lack specificity, prognostic value, and standardization across laboratories, and are not recommended for routine clinical use. Several hypotheses have been proposed regarding the pathogenesis of chronic idiopathic urticaria, but none provide definitive guidance for treatment or prognosis. The most widely accepted hypothesis involves histamine-releasing factors and defects in basophil signaling or function. Spontaneous remission occurs in 30–50% of patients within one year, with the average disease duration being two to five years. Up to 20% of patients may experience symptoms persisting beyond five years, and those with more severe symptoms tend to have a longer disease course. Patients with CSU often experience frustration and anxiety due to the chronic nature of the condition. Although no external cause is identified in most cases, various factors can exacerbate symptoms. Identifying and avoiding individual triggers is a critical component of effective management, and patient education should begin as soon as the diagnosis is made. First-line treatment for CSU involves the use of H1 antihistamines. Second-generation, less-sedating agents such as cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine, and desloratadine are preferred over older first-generation agents like hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, or mizolastine. Approximately 50% of patients may not achieve complete symptom control with standard doses of second-generation H1 antihistamines alone. For these non-responders, a stepwise approach to escalating therapy is appropriate. This includes increasing the dose of second-generation H1 antihistamines up to four times the standard dose, adding a different second-generation antihistamine, or introducing additional agents such as H2 antagonists, leukotriene receptor antagonists, or first-generation H1 antihistamines at bedtime. Patients should be informed about potential side effects, including sedation and anticholinergic effects, when using first-generation antihistamines. For patients with refractory symptoms, systemic glucocorticoids may be used for short-term control. If symptoms persist despite stepwise therapy or if dose escalation of first-generation H1 antihistamines is not tolerated, the disease is considered refractory. Once symptoms are controlled, maintenance therapy should be continued for at least one to three months before attempting to taper or discontinue medications. For patients with particularly difficult-to-control symptoms, the maintenance period may need to be extended. Andersen-Tawil syndrome (ATS), also known as Andersen syndrome or Long QT syndrome type 7, is a rare genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is caused by mutations in the KCNJ2 or KCNJ5 genes and is characterized by a triad of features: ventricular arrhythmias, periodic paralysis or muscle weakness, and skeletal dysmorphism (commonly including micrognathia and clinodactyly). The diagnosis of ATS is established in individuals with characteristic clinical and electrocardiographic findings and/or the identification of a pathogenic variant in the KCNJ2 gene. Molecular genetic testing approaches include single-gene testing, multigene panels, or comprehensive genomic testing (e.g., exome or genome sequencing), depending on the phenotype. Gene-targeted testing is more appropriate for individuals with distinct clinical features, while genomic testing is better suited for those with overlapping phenotypes. Suggestive findings for ATS include the presence of two of the following three criteria: periodic paralysis, symptomatic cardiac arrhythmias or electrocardiographic evidence of prolonged QTc or QUc intervals, and characteristic facial or skeletal features. Supportive findings include episodic weakness, abnormal serum potassium levels during attacks, and characteristic electrocardiographic abnormalities such as prominent U waves, prolonged Q-U intervals, and ventricular ectopy. Management of ATS requires a multidisciplinary approach involving neurologists and cardiologists familiar with periodic paralysis and cardiac arrhythmias, respectively. Treatment strategies include potassium supplementation to normalize serum potassium levels, lifestyle and dietary modifications to avoid known triggers, and the use of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide) to reduce attack frequency and severity. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators may be considered for patients with tachycardia-induced syncope. Flecainide, a type 1c antiarrhythmic agent, has shown promise in reducing ventricular arrhythmias in ATS. In a study of 10 individuals with confirmed KCNJ2 mutations, flecainide significantly reduced ventricular arrhythmias and suppressed exercise-induced arrhythmias. Patients followed for a mean of 23 months experienced no syncope or cardiac arrest. Preventive measures include avoiding medications that prolong the QT interval, potassium-wasting diuretics, and other agents that may exacerbate symptoms. Relatives at risk should undergo genetic testing or detailed neurologic and cardiologic evaluation to enable early diagnosis and treatment.
